questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: Name the two Houses of the Indian Parliament.
key_points: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
House of People and Council of States
Upper House and Lower House

factual_anchors.context: one of the two Houses that must be named for full credit
the second House required to complete the answer

questions.scheme_text: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha / House of People and Council of States / Upper House and Lower House.
questions.model_answer: The two Houses of the Indian Parliament are the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates answered it correctly. Some candidates either mentioned the three constituents of the Indian Parliament or the houses of the State Legislature.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the two sets of authority in a federal set up and the difference between the Union and the State governments.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: What is meant by the term 'Session'?
key_points: A period during which the House meets to conduct its business
Normally three sessions
The House meets at least twice
Budget or Summer Session, Winter Session and Monsoon Session

factual_anchors.context: the standard count of parliamentary sessions in a year

questions.scheme_text: The session means a period during which the House meets to conduct its business. / Normally three sessions. / The House meets at least twice. / Budget or Summer Session, Winter Session and Monsoon Session. [Any two sessions can be mentioned]
questions.model_answer: A Session is the period during which the House meets to conduct its business. Normally there are three sessions a year, and the House meets at least twice.
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates mentioned the three terms or the gap between two sessions whereas the question sought an answer to the meaning of the term Session.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Discuss the meaning of the term 'Session' in detail.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: How is the Speaker of the Lok Sabha elected?
key_points: The speaker is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha
He should be one amongst the members
By simple majority of members present and voting
questions.scheme_text: The speaker is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha / He should be one amongst the members / by simple majority of members present and voting.
questions.model_answer: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha from amongst themselves, by a simple majority of the members present and voting.
questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates wrote the correct answer to this question.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Make it clear to the students that the Speaker is elected "from among" the members of the house and by simple majority.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: What is the term of office of a Rajya Sabha member?

questions.model_answer: The term of office of a Rajya Sabha member is 6 years; one-third of its members retire every two years.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of the candidates answered the question correctly. However, a few candidates either mentioned the term of office of a Lok Sabha member instead of a Rajya Sabha member or wrote that the Rajya Sabha being a permanent house, is not subjected to dissolution.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Apprise students that 5 years is the normal term of office of the Vice President of India and the tenure of the Lok Sabha.

the second writ-issuing court required

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: Mention any one advantage of the Lok Adalat.
key_points: Saves time/speedy justice/fast/quick
Saves money/inexpensive/cheap/economical/no court fee / the fee will be refunded if case is settled
Lessens the burdens on the other courts/reduces backlog
Works on a spirit of compromise/no ill feeling/decision is binding on both the parties
Can move application on a plain paper/can pass awards regarding those cases which are at pre-litigation stage
Decisions are final and binding/No appeal in any court against decision
Promotes social justice or justice for weaker sections
questions.scheme_text: Advantages of the Lok Adalat: Saves time/speedy justice/fast/quick. / Saves money/inexpensive/cheap/economical/no court fee / the fee will be refunded if case is settled. / lessens the burdens on the other courts/reduces backlog. / Works on a spirit of compromise/no ill feeling/decision is binding on both the parties. / Can move application on a plain paper/can pass awards regarding those cases which are at pre-litigation stage. / Decisions are final and binding/No appeal in any court against decision / Promotes social justice or justice for weaker sections. (Any one point)
questions.model_answer: One advantage of the Lok Adalat is that it saves time and money, offering quick and inexpensive justice to the parties.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was attempted well by most candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Discuss the advantages of the Lok Adalat. Emphasise on all points.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: Mention any two contributions of Bipin Chandra Pal in promoting Nationalism.
key_points: Role of journalist
Worked for Bengal Public Opinion
The Tribune / New India to propagate nationalism
Founder of Vande Mataram
Wrote New Economic Menace to India
Wrote Spirit of Indian Nationalism
Advocated National Education
Aroused nationalistic passions or patriotism
Wanted National Education to be the basis of the freedom movement
Opposed the Caste system/worked for social progress
Advocated widow remarriage
Educated women
Participated in several Congress Sessions
Pleaded for Arms Act to be repealed
Contributed to promote national consciousness
Played an active role in anti-partition movement
Participated in Swadeshi movement
Proposed remedies to eradicate poverty
Wanted Swadeshi and Boycott to become means of freedom
Was against only Non-Cooperation Movement / wanted more action or aggressive measures
Was called The Father of Revolutionary thought in India

factual_anchors.context: the subject of the question; his specific contributions are being tested
a specific journal founded by Pal, valid as a contribution point
a specific publication used by Pal to propagate nationalism

questions.scheme_text: Any two contributions of Bipin Chandra Pal: Role of journalist / worked for Bengal Public Opinion. / The Tribune / New India to propagate nationalism. / Founder of Vande Mataram. / Wrote New Economic Menace to India. / Wrote Spirit of Indian Nationalism. / Advocated National Education. / aroused nationalistic passions or patriotism. / wanted National Education to be the basis of the freedom movement. / Opposed the Caste system/worked for social progress. / Advocated widow remarriage. / Educated women. / participated in several Congress Sessions. / Pleaded for Arms Act to be repealed. / contributed to promote national consciousness. / played an active role in anti-partition movement. / participated in Swadeshi movement. / proposed remedies to eradicate poverty. / wanted Swadeshi and Boycott to become means of freedom. / was against only Non-Cooperation Movement / wanted more action or aggressive measures. / Was called The Father of Revolutionary thought in India. questions.model_answer: Bipin Chandra Pal worked as a journalist, writing for publications such as Bengal Public Opinion and The Tribune to spread nationalist ideas, and he founded Vande Mataram to propagate nationalism.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of the candidates mentioned the contributions of Bipin Chandra Pal in promoting Nationalism correctly. However, a few got confused with the points of contribution of other nationalists.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Prepare a classification chart to teach students about the contributions of the 6 nationalists. Instruct them to specify the contributions of each of the nationalists under subheadings. Thus, a comparative study of the contribution of the nationalist leaders would be available for ready reference.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: State any two methods adopted by the Early Nationalists in the National Movement.
key_points: Held meetings
Speeches were made
Made use of the press, newspapers and journals
Criticized government policies
Sent memorandums
Sent petitions to government officials and the British parliament
Petitions, prayers, and protest through constitutional methods / 3Ps
Peaceful propaganda
Adopted constitutional means
Held discussions
Held processions
Passed resolutions
United public opinion
Sent deputations and delegations
Distribution of leaflets and pamphlets
questions.scheme_text: Held meetings / Speeches were made / Made use of the press, newspapers and journals / Criticized government policies. / Sent memorandums / sent petitions to government officials and the British parliament. / Petitions, prayers, and protest through constitutional methods. / 3Ps / peaceful propaganda / adopted constitutional means / held discussions / held processions / passed resolutions / United public opinion / sent deputations and delegations / distribution of leaflets and pamphlets. (Any two points)
questions.model_answer: The Early Nationalists held meetings and made speeches to voice their demands, and they made use of the press, newspapers and journals to criticise government policies and mobilise public opinion.
questions.examiner_comment: This subpart was well attempted by most candidates. However, a few wrote 'objectives' or got confused with the methods adopted by the Aggressive Nationalists instead of methods adopted by Early Nationalists.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Clarify the distinction between the Early Nationalists and Assertive Nationalists in their methods, objectives and beliefs. A classification chart with 4 points of differences between the two would help students at a glance, to note the differences.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: Why is October 16, 1905 regarded as an important day in the history of the Indian National Movement?

Congress felt it was a scheme of divide and rule policy

questions.examiner_comment: This subpart was well attempted by most candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the Partition of Bengal as a chronological event.

questions.subject: history_civics

key_points: Khilafat movement
Rowlatt Act/Black Act or Black Bill
Jallianwala Bagh tragedy/Massacre at Amritsar

an accepted cause of the Non-Cooperation Movement

questions.subject: history_civics

With the help of youth workers, peasants and radical organizations
Reorganization of agriculture and industry on socialist lines
Abolition of the zamindari system
Introduction of a new monetary and credit system
Establishment of a socialist society
Social ownership and control of both production and distribution

factual_anchors.context: the organisation whose objectives the question asks for

questions.scheme_text: Objectives of Forward Bloc: Liberation of India /freedom of India / With the help of youth workers, peasants and radical organizations / Reorganization of agriculture and industry on socialist lines / Abolition of the zamindari system / Introduction of a new monetary and credit system / Establishment of a socialist society / Social ownership and control of both production and distribution (Any two points)
questions.model_answer: Two objectives of the Forward Bloc were the liberation of India with the support of workers, peasants and youth, and the reorganisation of agriculture and industry on socialist lines.
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates confused the objectives of the Forward Bloc with the objectives of the INA. A few mentioned only one objective.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the objectives of INA and the Forward Bloc, clearly distinguishing between the two.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: What was meant by the term 'Imperialism', as a cause for World War I?
key_points: A system by which a powerful nation used to establish its control over another country
By political pressure
Infiltration and annexation
By outright wars
Supremacy over weaker countries
Establish colonies
Mad scramble among European nations for new territories in Asia and Africa
Morocco Crisis/Any other example of conquests

factual_anchors.context: a valid example of imperial conquest illustrating the answer

questions.scheme_text: A system by which a powerful nation used to establish its control over another country / By political pressure / Infiltration and annexation / By outright wars. / Supremacy over weaker countries / Establish colonies / Mad scramble among European nations for new territories in Asia and Africa / Morocco Crisis/Any other example of conquests. (Any one point)
questions.model_answer: Imperialism refers to a system by which a powerful nation established control over another country, through political pressure, infiltration, annexation, or outright war, in order to gain supremacy over weaker nations and establish colonies — as seen in the scramble for territories in Asia and Africa.
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates confused 'imperialism' with 'aggressive nationalism'. A large number of candidates gave the meaning as "extreme love for one's country and hatred for other."
questions.teacher_suggestion: Clarify Imperialism, its meaning and significance with examples for better comprehension.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Union Legislature, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Explain any three Legislative powers of the Union Parliament.
key_points: To make laws on the union list /97 subjects
Matters in the concurrent list/47 subjects
Residuary powers/matters not mentioned in 3 lists
Matters in the state list
During an emergency
Approved by 2/3 majority by the Rajya Sabha
When two or more states ask
President's Rule
Ordinances must be approved
Powers during emergency/67 subjects in state list

factual_anchors.context: the count of Union List subjects; a specific numeric anchor
the count of Concurrent List subjects; a specific numeric anchor
the Rajya Sabha majority enabling Parliament to legislate on state subjects

questions.scheme_text: Legislative powers of the union parliament: To make laws on the union list /97 subjects / Matters in the concurrent list/47 subjects / Residuary powers/matters not mentioned in 3 lists / Matters in the state list / during an emergency / approved by 2/3 majority by the Rajya Sabha / when two or more states ask / President's Rule / Ordinances must be approved / Powers during emergency/67 subjects in state list. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: The Union Parliament can make laws on subjects in the Union List, on subjects in the Concurrent List, and it also holds residuary powers over matters not mentioned in any of the three lists.
questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates wrote the three Legislative powers of the Union Parliament correctly. However, a few confused Legislative powers with Executive powers.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the meaning of the words Legislation, Legislative and Executive powers of the Parliament in detail to students.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Union Legislature, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: State any three exclusive powers of the Lok Sabha that is not enjoyed by the other House.
key_points: Motions of No-Confidence against the government can only be introduced and passed in the Lok Sabha/answerable to the Lok Sabha only/ enjoy power only until they enjoy the trust of the house
Money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend it /budget is passed/controls the national purse/has complete control over finance
In case of a deadlock between the two houses, the will of the Lok Sabha prevails due to its higher numerical strength
Can pass an Adjournment Motion

factual_anchors.context: the House whose exclusive powers are being tested
the contrasting House that does not enjoy these powers

questions.scheme_text: Motions of No-Confidence against the government can only be introduced and passed in the Lok Sabha/answerable to the Lok Sabha only/ enjoy power only until they enjoy the trust of the house / Money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend it /budget is passed/controls the national purse/has complete control over finance / In case of a deadlock between the two houses, the will of the Lok Sabha prevails due to its higher numerical strength. / Can pass an Adjournment Motion. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Motions of No-Confidence against the government can only be introduced and passed in the Lok Sabha. Money Bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend them. In case of a deadlock between the two Houses, the will of the Lok Sabha prevails owing to its higher numerical strength.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of the candidates wrote the correct answer. A few candidates wrote about the general powers and got confused between the powers of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. A few could not understand the word 'exclusive'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Clarify the word 'exclusive' and explain the exclusive powers of both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha thoroughly to the students, giving reasons.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Union Legislature, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: List any four functions of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
key_points: Regulate the proceedings of the house
Certifies a bill as money bill
Maintains discipline in the house
Puts issues to vote and announces results
Does not vote in the house except when there is a tie /casting vote
Presides over the joint session of the parliament
Presides over meetings
Recognises a member on the floor of the house
Asks a member to yield the floor
Preserves order in the house
Expunges unparliamentary words
Receives all petitions
Decides the order of speeches
Decides which questions to admit
Communicates the decision of the house to the authorities
Can adjourn the house
Decides whether there is any breach of privilege or contempt of house
Regulates the press and visitors
Appoints chairmen of various parliamentary committees
Disqualifies members under anti defection law
All bills are signed by him
Interprets the rules of the house
questions.scheme_text: Functions of the Speaker of Lok Sabha: Regulate the proceedings of the house / Certifies a bill as money bill / Maintains discipline in the house / Puts issues to vote and announces results / Does not vote in the house except when there is a tie /casting vote / Presides over the joint session of the parliament. / presides over meetings / recognises a member on the floor of the house / asks a member to yield the floor / preserves order in the house / expunges unparliamentary words / receives all petitions / decides the order of speeches / decides which questions to admit / communicates the decision of the house to the authorities / can adjourn the house / decides whether there is any breach of privilege or contempt of house / regulates the press and visitors / appoints chairmen of various parliamentary committees / disqualifies members under anti defection law / all bills are signed by him / interprets the rules of the house. (Any four points)
questions.model_answer: The Speaker regulates the proceedings of the House, certifies a bill as a Money Bill, maintains discipline in the House, and puts issues to vote and announces the results.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was answered well by the candidates in general.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Executive Power of the Indian Union is vested in the President. In this context, answer the following:
questions.question_text: How is the President of India elected? State the composition of the Electoral College that elects him.
key_points: President is elected indirectly by the members of an electoral college /single transferable vote/proportional representation
Elected members of both houses [LS and RS] of parliament
Elected members of the legislative assemblies of the states including the national capital territory of Delhi and the union territory of Puducherry
OR MPs and MLAs

factual_anchors.context: the body electing the President; central to the answer
the National Capital Territory whose MLAs are part of the Electoral College
the Union Territory whose MLAs are part of the Electoral College

questions.scheme_text: 1. President is elected indirectly by the members of an electoral college. /single transferable vote/proportional representation. 2. Composition of Electoral college: Elected members of both houses [LS and RS] of parliament / Elected members of the legislative assemblies of the states including the national capital territory of Delhi and the union territory of Puducherry. / OR MPs and MLAs
questions.model_answer: The President of India is elected indirectly by the members of an Electoral College, through a single transferable vote and proportional representation. This College is composed of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States, including the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry.
questions.examiner_comment: This subpart was attempted well by most candidates. Some wrote that the President is elected by Direct elections. Some candidates did not give the composition of the Electoral College correctly.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Identify technical terms such as Electoral College, etc. to be used in Civics and explain the meaning of these terms to the students in detail.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Executive Power of the Indian Union is vested in the President. In this context, answer the following:
questions.question_text: Explain any three Discretionary Powers of the President.
key_points: Where he uses his wisdom and judgement
Dissolution of Lok Sabha during constitutional crisis
Explore possibilities of alternative government at the centre
Dismissal of ministers when the government collapses due to No confidence
Appointment of the PM where no single party commands
Appointment of PM in case of death
May withhold assent to an ordinary bill or send it back for reconsideration
No time limit within which he is to declare his assent/refusal of bill
questions.scheme_text: The discretionary powers: Where he uses his wisdom and judgement. / Dissolution of Lok Sabha during constitutional crisis / Explore possibilities of alternative government at the centre / Dismissal of ministers when the government collapses due to No confidence. / Appointment of the PM where no single party commands / Appointment of PM in case of death / May withhold assent to an ordinary bill or send it back for reconsideration / No time limit within which he is to declare his assent/refusal of bill. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: The President's discretionary powers include the dissolution of the Lok Sabha during a constitutional crisis, the appointment of a Prime Minister when no single party commands a majority, and the power to withhold assent to an ordinary bill or send it back for reconsideration.
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates did not write the Discretionary Powers of the President correctly.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the meaning of the term 'Discretion', before explaining the powers of the President, under this category. Teach the discretionary powers of the President with instances.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Executive Power of the Indian Union is vested in the President. In this context, answer the following:
questions.question_text: Mention any four Executive Powers of the President.
key_points: Head of the Union administration/administration of the country runs in his house/All orders are issued in his name
Appointment of officials of the state

Appoints the Attorney General, Auditor General, Ambassador, Members of UPSC, Judges of High Court and Supreme Court, Members of the Planning Commission, Election Commissioner, Governors of State, PM and the Council of Ministers
Control over state governments during emergency
And Union territories and border areas/exercises power through an administrator appointed by the President

factual_anchors.context: a valid example of an official appointed by the President
a valid example of a body whose members the President appoints

questions.scheme_text: The Executive powers: Head of the Union administration/administration of the country runs in his house/All orders are issued in his name / Appointment of officials of the state / Appoints the Attorney General, Auditor General, Ambassador, Members of UPSC, Judges of High Court and Supreme Court, Members of the Planning Commission, Election Commissioner, Governors of State, PM and the Council of Ministers. / Control over state governments during emergency / And Union territories and border areas/exercises power through an administrator appointed by the President. (Any four points)
questions.model_answer: The President's Executive powers include heading the Union administration, with all orders issued in his name; appointing officials such as the Attorney General, the Auditor General and the judges of the High Courts and Supreme Court; and exercising control over State governments during an emergency and over Union Territories through an administrator.
questions.examiner_comment: A large number of candidates answered this part correctly. However, some candidates mixed up the Legislative and the Executive powers. A few candidates confused the Executive powers with the Emergency powers of the President.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Clarify the distinction between the Executive powers and Legislative powers of the President.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Supreme Court as the Apex Court in our Indian Judiciary, explain the following:
questions.question_text: Any three cases that come under the Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
key_points: Centre state
Interstate disputes
Union and state on one side and other states on other side
Protection of Fundamental rights
Transfer of cases from lower courts
Interpretation of constitution
questions.scheme_text: Original Jurisdiction: Centre state / interstate disputes / Union and state on one side and other states on other side / Protection of Fundamental rights / Transfer of cases from lower courts / Interpretation of constitution (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: The Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court covers disputes between the Centre and a State, disputes between two or more States, and cases involving the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
questions.examiner_comment: Most candidates attempted this part of the question well. However, a few got confused with the Appellate and other jurisdictions.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Teach students the meaning of the Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme court.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Supreme Court as the Apex Court in our Indian Judiciary, explain the following:
questions.question_text: Power of Judicial Review.
key_points: The Supreme Court is the interpreter of the Constitution
It has the power to review laws passed by the union or state legislatures or executive
The Supreme Court can declare a law ultra vires or null and void, if it is against the letter and spirit of the Constitution or contravenes any provision of the constitution

factual_anchors.context: the court exercising the power of judicial review

questions.scheme_text: Power of Judicial Review: The Supreme Court is the interpreter of the Constitution. / It has the power to review laws passed by the union or state legislatures or executive. / The Supreme Court can declare a law ultra vires or null and void, if it is against the letter and spirit of the Constitution or contravenes any provision of the constitution.
questions.model_answer: The Supreme Court, as the interpreter of the Constitution, has the power to review laws passed by the Union or State legislatures or the executive, and it can declare a law ultra vires — null and void — if it contravenes the letter or spirit of the Constitution.
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates confused Judicial Review with Revisory Jurisdiction and hence could not explain the 'Power of the Judicial Review'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Spell out the meaning of the term 'Judicial Review' and explain how this power of the Judiciary can invalidate both the Executive and the Legislature when they go against the Constitution.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Supreme Court as the Apex Court in our Indian Judiciary, explain the following:
questions.question_text: Supreme Court as a Court of Record.
key_points: Its judgement and orders are preserved as a record
This can be produced in any court as precedents
Future references
Testimony
If a person commits a contempt of court, the court has the authority to punish contempt
The Supreme Court acts as the Guardian of the constitution
questions.scheme_text: The court of record has two implications: Its judgement and orders are preserved as a record. / This can be produced in any court as precedents. / future references / testimony / If a person commits a contempt of court, the court has the authority to punish contempt. / The Supreme Court acts as the Guardian of the constitution. (Any two points)
questions.model_answer: As a Court of Record, the Supreme Court's judgements and orders are permanently preserved as a record and can be produced in any court as precedents. In addition, if any person commits a contempt of court, the Supreme Court has the authority to punish that contempt, upholding its position as the Guardian of the Constitution.
questions.examiner_comment: This was a well attempted question.
questions.teacher_suggestion: While explaining Supreme Court as a Court of Record, lay stress on the keywords as 'records' and 'future reference'.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: By 1857, conditions were ripe for a mass uprising in the form of the Great Revolt of 1857. In this context, explain the following:

(Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Economic causes of the Revolt of 1857 included the exploitation of India's economic resources and the drain of wealth to Britain, the decay of cottage industries and handicrafts due to British imports, and the growing poverty and famines that impoverished the peasantry.
questions.examiner_comment: The subparts (a), (b) and (c) of this question were attempted well by most of the candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the causes of the Revolt of 1857 under sub-headings such as, Economic causes, Military causes, and Political causes.

(Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Military causes included the ill-treatment of Indian soldiers, who were treated as servants with a wide social distance from their British officers; the bleak prospects of promotion for Indian soldiers; and the introduction of the Enfield rifles, whose greased cartridges caused deep resentment.
questions.examiner_comment: The subparts (a), (b) and (c) of this question were attempted well by most of the candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the causes of the Revolt of 1857 under sub-headings such as, Economic causes, Military causes, and Political causes.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: By 1857, conditions were ripe for a mass uprising in the form of the Great Revolt of 1857. In this context, explain the following:

questions.examiner_comment: The subparts (a), (b) and (c) of this question were attempted well by most of the candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Conduct role play in class to make the topic more interesting.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Mass Phase of the National Movement under the leadership of Gandhi, answer the following:

78 persons followed him

On the morning of 6th of April, Gandhi violated the salt-laws by picking up some salt left by the sea-waves
Gandhi's signal to disobey the government law

factual_anchors.context: date Gandhi wrote to the Viceroy; a chronological anchor
date the march began from Sabarmati; a chronological anchor
date Gandhi reached Dandi; a chronological anchor
date the salt law was violated; a chronological anchor
the number of marchers who followed Gandhi
the starting point of the march
the coastal destination of the march

questions.scheme_text: On 2nd March 1930, Gandhi wrote a letter to the Viceroy / communicating his decision to start the Civil Disobedience Movement. / On 12th March began Mahatma Gandhi's historic march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, a village on the Gujarat seacoast / 78 persons followed him. / He reached Dandi on 5th April. / On the morning of 6th of April, Gandhi violated the salt-laws by picking up some salt left by the sea-waves. / Gandhi's signal to disobey the government law. questions.model_answer: On 2nd March 1930, Gandhi wrote to the Viceroy announcing his decision to launch the Civil Disobedience Movement. On 12th March, he began his historic march from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi, accompanied by 78 followers, reaching Dandi on 5th April. On the morning of 6th April, he violated the salt laws by picking up salt left by the sea-waves, signalling to the nation to disobey the government's law.

questions.teacher_suggestion: Narrate the event-the historic Dandi march from Sabarmati to Dandi and the subsequent violation of the salt Law point wise as it was an important day that marked the beginning of a non-violent Civil Disobedience Movement.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Mass Phase of the National Movement under the leadership of Gandhi, answer the following:
questions.question_text: State any three reasons for the launching of the Quit India Movement.
key_points: Failure of the Cripps Mission
Worsening of Communal Problem
Japan posed a serious threat to India

factual_anchors.context: its failure is a listed reason for launching Quit India
the year of the Quit India Movement

questions.scheme_text: Reasons for launching the Quit India Movement: Failure of the Cripps Mission / Worsening of Communal Problem / Japan posed a serious threat to India. (Any two points)
questions.model_answer: Two significant reasons for launching the Quit India Movement were the failure of the Cripps Mission to satisfy Indian demands, and the growing threat posed by the Japanese advance towards India's borders.
questions.examiner_comment: Several candidates wrote the reasons for the launching of the Quit India Movement such as 'economic distress', while some wrote the causes of other mass movements led by Gandhi such as the Non-Cooperation Movement and the Civil Disobedience Movement.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the political reasons in India as well as in the International arena during 1942 to help the students understand and comprehend the reasons for the passing of the Quit India Resolution and its significant effects.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Mass Phase of the National Movement under the leadership of Gandhi, answer the following:
questions.question_text: Explain any four significant effects of the Quit India Movement.
key_points: Important landmark - It saw disturbances practically all over India
It warned the British that they were not wanted in India/days were limited/collapse of authority
Demand from Indians that they could have nothing short of Independence
Quit India Movement strengthened the Congress Socialist Party
In the Quit India Movement, the Indian Revolution reached its climax
Led to political awakening
Indian problem attracted the attention of the world especially USA
Symbolic of new confidence among Indians
Demonstrated nationalistic feelings
Mass movement/last mass movement
United young and old and people of different religions and regions
No political activity till after the war ended in 1945

factual_anchors.context: the movement whose effects are being tested
the year the war ended, after which political activity resumed

questions.scheme_text: Significant consequences of the Quit India Movement: Important landmark - It saw disturbances practically all over India. / It warned the British that they were not wanted in India/days were limited/collapse of authority / Demand from Indians that they could have nothing short of Independence / Quit India Movement strengthened the Congress Socialist Party. / In the Quit India Movement, the Indian Revolution reached its climax. / Led to political awakening / Indian problem attracted the attention of the world especially USA / Symbolic of new confidence among Indians / Demonstrated nationalistic feelings / Mass movement/last mass movement / United young and old and people of different religions and regions / No political activity till after the war ended in 1945. (Any four points)
questions.model_answer: The Quit India Movement was an important landmark, as it saw disturbances practically all over India and warned the British that their days in India were numbered. It led to political awakening and demonstrated a new sense of confidence and nationalist feeling among Indians, uniting people of different ages, religions and regions in a mass movement.
questions.examiner_comment: Most of the candidates answered this question correctly. However, a few jumbled up the parts with the impact of the Non-Cooperation Movement and the Civil Disobedience Movement. Some candidates wrote that the British quit India and we gained independence as the effect of the Quit India Movement.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Ensure that students understand the three major Gandhian movements - Causes, Course and Consequences. Enhance the understanding of this topic through a role play or a skit.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Partition Plan, answer the following:

key_points: Lord Mountbatten
He came to India for the purpose of taking necessary steps for the transfer of power to the Indians
To restore peace among the two sections of Congress and the League
To present a plan for the partition

factual_anchors.context: the last Viceroy; the required answer to part (i)

questions.scheme_text: (i) Lord Mountbatten (ii) He came to India for the purpose of taking necessary steps for the transfer of power to the Indians. /To restore peace among the two sections of Congress and the League. /To present a plan for the partition.
questions.model_answer: The last Viceroy of India was Lord Mountbatten. He came to India to take the necessary steps for the transfer of power to the Indians, and to restore peace between the Congress and the Muslim League by presenting a plan for the partition of the country.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by the candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain each and every event related to the Partition Plan of India thoroughly to the students.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Partition Plan, answer the following:
questions.question_text: Mention any three proposals under his plan.
key_points: Partition - into two dominions
Relations between the two new Dominions - to decide what relation to have between each other and the commonwealth
A Boundary Commission - to settle the boundaries
Princely States - treaties would end, and they could decide to join either of the dominions or remain independent
Bengal & Punjab - legislative assemblies to decide
Sindh - legislative assembly to decide
N.W. Frontier Province - to decide by a referendum
District of Sylhet - to decide by a referendum
Constituent Assembly - separate Constituent assembly for both the parties
Transfer of Power - would take place before 1948

factual_anchors.context: the deadline before which transfer of power was to occur
a listed proposal under the Mountbatten Plan

questions.scheme_text: Three proposals under his Plan: Partition - into two dominions / Relations between the two new Dominions - to decide what relation to have between each other and the commonwealth / A Boundary Commission - to settle the boundaries / Princely States - treaties would end, and they could decide to join either of the dominions or remain independent / Bengal & Punjab - legislative assemblies to decide / Sindh - legislative assembly to decide / N.W. Frontier Province - to decide by a referendum / District of Sylhet - to decide by a referendum / Constituent Assembly - separate Constituent assembly for both the parties / Transfer of Power - would take place before 1948. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Under the Mountbatten Plan, India would be partitioned into two dominions; a Boundary Commission would be set up to settle the boundaries between them; and the legislative assemblies of Bengal and Punjab would decide whether their provinces should be partitioned.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of the candidates answered this part of the question correctly. However, some candidates wrote about the Cabinet Mission Plan or the Provisions of the Indian Independence Act.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Ensure that students understand the Cabinet Mission Plan, the Mountbatten Plan and the Provisions of the Indian Independence Act of 1947.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: With reference to the Partition Plan, answer the following:
questions.question_text: State any four reasons for the Congress to finally accept the Plan.
key_points: Large scale communal riots
League joined Interim government to obstruct and not to cooperate
Only alternative to Partition was a Federation with a weak centre
Any further continuation of British rule would mean a greater calamity for India /People and leaders were fed up with their rule in India/wanted to get rid of the British rule by paying any price
Further delay could find India in a Civil War
Leaders felt that partition would aid the Constitutions of separate electorates /and other undemocratic procedures
questions.scheme_text: Acceptance of Plan: Large scale communal riots / League joined Interim government to obstruct and not to cooperate. / Only alternative to Partition was a Federation with a weak centre. / Any further continuation of British rule would mean a greater calamity for India. /People and leaders were fed up with their rule in India/wanted to get rid of the British rule by paying any price. / Further delay could find India in a Civil War. / Leaders felt that partition would aid the Constitutions of separate electorates. /and other undemocratic procedures. (Any four points)
questions.model_answer: The Congress finally accepted the Plan because large-scale communal riots had broken out across the country; the Muslim League had joined the interim government only to obstruct its functioning; the only alternative to partition was a federation with a weak centre; and any further delay threatened to plunge India into civil war.
questions.examiner_comment: Some candidates found it difficult to write four reasons why the Congress finally accepted the Plan.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Advise students to study the clauses of above-mentioned Plans /Act thoroughly and present them in a factual manner.
